name: Relational databases
summary: Tables, SQL and transactions: the dependable default.
howItWorks: A relational database stores data in tables with a defined schema and relationships between them. You query it with SQL, join across tables, and group changes into ACID transactions so they all happen or none do. Managed services handle backups, failover, patching and read replicas that take read-heavy queries off the primary.
analogy: A meticulous accountant’s ledger. Every entry follows the rules, the books always balance, and you can ask it almost any question.
useWhen: Most business data: users, orders, inventory, billing
Data with relationships you want to query flexibly
Anything where correctness matters more than raw write speed
avoidWhen: Billions of tiny writes a day with simple access patterns; consider key-value or time-series
Scanning petabytes for analytics, which belongs in a warehouse
example: An online store keeps customers, orders and order lines in PostgreSQL. Placing an order inserts the order and decrements stock in one transaction. Finance reports run on a read replica so they don’t slow checkout.

providers.azure: Azure SQL Database, Azure Database for PostgreSQL
providers.oss: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB; also PlanetScale (hosted Vitess MySQL and Postgres) and CockroachDB (distributed SQL that speaks the Postgres protocol; proprietary licence since 2024), Neon (serverless Postgres, owned by Databricks), Vitess (sharding for MySQL, a CNCF project) CedarDB (Postgres-compatible, for transactions and analytics, proprietary) and Turso (a SQLite-compatible rewrite in Rust with concurrent writes, MIT; Supabase is acquiring the company); self-run Postgres usually adds Patroni for failover and WAL-G for backups, and on Kubernetes an operator such as CloudNativePG, Crunchy’s PGO or the Percona Operators runs the cluster

COMMIT;   -- both changes happen, or neither does
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY orders DESC LIMIT 10;

diagram.caption: The app reads and writes the primary. The primary streams its changes to a read replica, and reporting queries go to the replica instead.

story: By the late 1960s, databases stored records as trees, like IBM’s IMS, released around 1968, or as networks of linked records, like the CODASYL model that Charles Bachman championed. Programs found data by following those links, so changing how data was stored meant changing the programs. In June 1970 Edgar F. “Ted” Codd, at IBM’s San Jose Research Laboratory, published “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks”. He argued that users “must be protected from having to know how the data is organized in the machine”, and proposed storing data as tables (relations) queried through one general language.

IBM was slow to commit, and until 1984 it treated IMS as its serious database. Its System R project in San Jose, begun in 1974, produced SEQUEL (later SQL), designed by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and set out to show that a relational system could have the full function and performance needed for everyday production use. At Berkeley, Michael Stonebraker’s team built Ingres. Relational Software, now Oracle, shipped Oracle V2, one of the first commercial SQL databases, in 1979, Codd won the Turing Award in 1981, and SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986.

Relational databases became the default home for business data, and open-source MySQL and PostgreSQL carried them into the web era. The cloud turned them into a service: Amazon RDS launched in 2009 as managed MySQL, and later systems such as Google Spanner (2012) and Amazon Aurora DSQL (2025) spread transactional databases across data centers and Regions.

choices.choice: Tables of values instead of stored pointers
choices.why: A main goal of Codd’s paper was data independence: programs should keep working when the storage layout changes. Relationships are expressed by matching values, such as a customer ID, not by links baked into the files.

choices.choice: Say what you want, not how to find it
choices.why: A query describes the result, and the database chooses the indexes and join order. System R’s cost-based optimizer made that choice automatically; its inventor, Patricia Selinger, said cost-based optimization “made relational work”. It also means the same SQL keeps working as data and indexes change.

choices.choice: Transactions that happen completely or not at all
choices.why: Orders, payments and stock levels must never be half-updated. System R logged every change so it could undo incomplete transactions after a failure, while aiming for performance comparable to existing systems.

IBM’s backing moved the industry to SQL over alternatives like Ingres’s QUEL, and ANSI and ISO standards followed. No database claims full conformance to the current core standard, but skills and tools carry over between databases.

timeline.text: Codd publishes the relational model at IBM San Jose
IBM’s System R project begins; SEQUEL, later SQL, is designed
Oracle V2, one of the first commercial SQL databases, ships
SQL becomes an ANSI standard, and ISO follows in 1987
Amazon RDS offers managed MySQL in the cloud
Google’s Spanner paper describes a globally distributed, synchronously replicated database
Amazon Aurora DSQL, a multi-Region distributed SQL database, becomes generally available
